excerpt: With Google Authenticator, you can synchronize your verification codes across all your devices, simply by signing in to your Google Account.
When you first open the app, tap Use without an account.
On your old device, create a QR code... On your new device, tap Scan QR code
When you sign in to your Google Account within Google Authenticator on a new device, your codes are automatically synced to this device.
Authenticator can sync codes for multiple Google Accounts and display them from the same mobile device.
To edit your Authenticator code on Android, swipe left on any code to show the edit option.
To organize your Authenticator codes, touch and hold any code, then drag to reorder to a desired location.
To delete an Authenticator code on Android, swipe right on any code to show the delete option.

I recently had a broken phone replaced and had depended on a backup to have my TOTP keys on my new phone. It was not a part of the phone backup. :(
Years ago I updated authenticator and it wiped out all my entries, which led to an incredibly aggravating week of account recovery.
Too little too late. Everyone I know has moved to 1password or authy or yubikeys (or some combination). I'll never understand why they didn't do this many years ago.

Google's authenticator has been outright harmful in how neglected it has been, especially when it comes to backing up your codes outside the app... For years I've been telling anyone who'd listen to use Authy instead.
And it only took them 12 years to do it. Authy had already implemented syncing to different devices for a long while.
Storing it in the google cloud doesn't satisfy me. I just simply want the codes under my control... google still makes it stupendously difficult to just get a simple text export to a file.
If Google ever decides to kick you out of your account, Authenticator data will be gone. Google has done this on several occasions in the past.
Does that mean one can use adb to backup Google Authenticator's data as well? Last time I tried, the app data was explicitly marked as excluded in backups.
Google Authenticator already has a QR-Code based very easy export procedure, I just backup my GAuth to my spare phone and tablet. It feels safer because it's physical.
tl;dr if a hacker gets access to your Google account it'll be like you didn't have 2FA at all
Authy gets this right. Not sure why anyone would trust Google with their 2FA secrets.
Imagine your google account getting deleted cuz you got banned from Google and the suddenly you lose all your 2FA secrets cuz they are part of that account
Don't upgrade! I just had this unpleasant experience and warned everyone... Warning: Google Authenticator upgrade loses all accounts.
Every time I upgraded to a new iOS 7 beta, it wiped my Google Authenticator account tokens... I can't log in to my CampBX account anymore.
Google Auth 2.0 redefines two-factor auth: something you know + something you DON'T have. Their entire purpose in life is this second part and they completely and absolutely botched it.
For those looking for Google Authenticator alternatives, I recommend either Duo Mobile from Duo Security or Authy. I ditched Google Authenticator a while ago and haven't missed it one bit.

Google Authenticator does not allow you to include your codes in your backup, even when it's encrypted. So due to Google Authenticator, losing your 2fa codes is an expected problem and many companies allow you to reset it by simply calling them.

Google Authenticator has a feature to allow export of all saved codes into one QR code for re-import into Google Authenticator running on another device. I printed a copy of my export QR code for use in case my device is lost or stolen.
A user had a broken phone replaced and expected a backup to restore their TOTP keys on the new phone, but the Authenticator codes were not part of the phone backup.
Prefers not to put 2FA codes in the cloud. Says Google Authenticator's QR-code export is very easy, and uses it to back up GAuth to a spare phone and tablet, which feels safer because it's physical.
Years ago an Authenticator update wiped out all of this user's entries, which led to an incredibly aggravating week of account recovery.

Complains that Google put push-approval logic in other apps instead of Authenticator. Before the company adopted Okta, users got prompts like 'Open the YouTube app on your phone to approve this login' even when Authenticator was installed.

Says the app finally allows export to a QR code, but Google still makes it stupendously difficult to get a simple text export to a file. Works around this by saving the otpauth code for each account from the start.
Says Google Authenticator has been outright harmful in how neglected it has been, especially for backing up codes outside the app, and has told people for years to use Authy instead.

Google Authenticator's export QR code bundles multiple accounts. Another instance of GA can read it, but other TOTP apps might not. Workaround: screenshot every setup QR code and store the images safely for migration.
Last time this user tried, Google Authenticator's app data was explicitly excluded from adb backups. They started saving the secrets elsewhere because otherwise they couldn't have any backup at all.
Complains that the new Authenticator cloud sync doesn't get the same end-to-end encryption as Android backups. Wants at least an option to use the normal Android backup system.
On privacy concerns about the cloud sync: you can just log out in the app to stop the synchronization. With a second device, you can use the app's QR export/import instead.

'How does Google Authenticator work? Really poorly.' Says this matches app store reviews, where it has a sub-2.5-star rating. Notes that until recently you couldn't back up passcodes, making it extremely risky, and recommends Authy.
Warning (2013, iOS): upgrading Google Authenticator lost all accounts. The poster says the update 'completely and absolutely botched' the app's core purpose, with no warning in the release notes.
Every iOS 7 beta upgrade wiped this user's Google Authenticator tokens. Google and Dropbox let them move 2FA, but they could no longer log in to their CampBX account. They switched to Authy.

Reports that the new Google Authenticator version crashes 100% reproducibly when you scan two QR codes in a row on iOS 7. Recommends keeping backups of otpauth:// URLs, e.g. in a password-protected archive or printed as QR codes.
On rooted Android, this user accessed Google Authenticator's sqlite key database directly to copy their keys from phone to tablet.
A user who offers 2FA says providers told them they were getting a surge in support calls because of the Authenticator app update.

Defends Google Authenticator. Says the lack of backup and sync is a feature, not a bug, because sync adds attack surface. A simple app like GA has a far smaller attack surface than Authy, LastPass or 1Password, and lower risk of compromised updates.

This user's Google Authenticator data survived a phone migration only by rooting the new phone and restoring app data with Titanium Backup. They note this isn't something a normal user would be expected to do.
Settled on Aegis, which exports secrets to an encrypted file. Says it is a bit more tedious than Authy-style cloud sync, but less tedious to back up than Google Authenticator.
Argues the case against Google Authenticator is overstated: 'if you use Authenticator, just keep using it, it's fine.' Points out that Authy codes were by default susceptible to SIM-swap attacks.
